title: The Book of Deuteronomy Timeline
sub: Moses's Farewell · The Law Renewed on the Plains of Moab
desc: On the edge of the promised land he will never enter, Moses retells forty years of wilderness history, restates the law for a new generation, and sets blessing and curse before Israel one final time — closing with a prophetic song, a blessing on all twelve tribes, and his own death on Mount Nebo.

eras.label: Era One · Deuteronomy 1
eras.name: Moses Recaps the Journey From Horeb
eras.dates: On the plains of Moab, Moses opens his farewell address by retelling forty years of history — the appointment of judges, the twelve spies, and Israel's fear-driven refusal to enter the land that cost an entire generation its future.

events.title: Judges Appointed at Horeb
events.detail: Moses recalls appointing capable leaders over groups of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens to share the judicial burden of the growing nation, instructing them to judge fairly "whether between one person and a native Israelite or a resident foreigner."

events.title: The Spies, and a Generation's Refusal
events.detail: Moses retells the story of the twelve spies and Israel's terrified refusal to enter Canaan despite the land being genuinely good, recalling God's resulting oath that none of that generation except Caleb — and Moses himself, for his own separate failure — would see the promised land.

verses.text: “Not a single person of this evil generation will see the good land that I promised to give to your ancestors! The exception is Caleb son of Jephunneh; he will see it… because he has wholeheartedly followed me.”

eras.label: Era Two · Deuteronomy 2
eras.name: Past Edom and Moab, and Victory Over Sihon
eras.dates: Moses recounts forty years of respecting boundaries — refusing to provoke Edom, Moab, and Ammon over land God had already assigned to Lot's and Esau's descendants — before Sihon's stubborn refusal to grant passage triggers Israel's first decisive military victory.

events.title: Respecting Esau's, Moab's, and Ammon's Territory
events.detail: Moses recalls God's explicit instructions not to provoke Edom, Moab, or Ammon, since their land had already been assigned to Lot's and Esau's descendants — even noting how those nations had themselves displaced earlier peoples, the Rephaites and Horites, just as Israel would soon do in Canaan.

events.title: Sihon's Land Conquered
events.detail: A peaceful request for passage through Sihon's territory is refused because God "made him obstinate and stubborn"; Israel defeats him decisively and takes his cities, sparing nothing but the livestock and plunder.

eras.label: Era Three · Deuteronomy 3
eras.name: Victory Over Og, and Moses Barred From the Land
eras.dates: A second decisive victory, over the giant king Og of Bashan, completes Israel's conquest of the Transjordan — but Moses's own personal request to cross into Canaan is flatly denied, leaving him only a view from a mountaintop.

events.title: Og of Bashan Defeated
events.detail: Israel defeats Og of Bashan, whose massive iron bed (or sarcophagus) still stood on display in Ammon at the time of writing, completing Israel's conquest of the entire Transjordan region.

events.title: "Enough of That!" — Moses Denied Entry
events.detail: Moses allocates the conquered Transjordan land to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, then recalls pleading with God to let him cross the Jordan — a request God cuts off sharply, permitting him only to view the land from a mountaintop before commissioning Joshua to lead the actual conquest.

verses.text: “The LORD was angry at me because of you and would not listen to me. Instead, he said to me, ‘Enough of that! Do not speak to me anymore about this matter. Go up to the top of Pisgah and take a good look.’”

eras.label: Era Four · Deuteronomy 4
eras.name: "You Saw No Form" — a Call to Exclusive Worship
eras.dates: Moses grounds Israel's entire prohibition on idols in a specific historical memory — at Sinai they heard God's voice but saw no visible shape at all — and warns that forgetting this will eventually scatter them among the nations, though even there repentance will bring restoration.

events.title: "You Saw No Form… Do Not Corrupt Yourselves"
events.detail: Moses insists Israel saw no visible form of God at Horeb, only heard his voice — the theological basis for the prohibition against images — and warns that making any image would provoke "the LORD your God, a consuming fire, a jealous God" to swift and severe judgment.

verses.text: “The LORD [Yahweh] your God [Elohim] is a fire consuming he, a jealous God [El].”

events.title: Scattered, Yet Never Forgotten
events.detail: Moses predicts Israel's eventual idolatry and exile among the nations as inevitable if they forget the covenant, yet promises that genuine repentance even there will move the merciful God to remember his ancient covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

verses.text: “You will know this day and take it to heart that the LORD [Yahweh] is God [Elohim] in the heavens above and on the earth below — there is no other!”

eras.label: Era Five · Deuteronomy 5
eras.name: The Ten Commandments Repeated
eras.dates: Moses restates the Ten Commandments word for word to the new generation who did not personally stand at Sinai, reminding them of the terror that made them beg Moses to serve as the go-between rather than hear God's voice directly.

events.title: "Not With Our Fathers, but With Us"
events.detail: Moses restates the Ten Commandments to a generation who did not personally experience Sinai, insisting the covenant applies directly to "us, we who are here today" — and recalls how the people's own terror at hearing God's voice led them to ask Moses to mediate every future word from God.

verses.text: “You go near so that you can hear everything the LORD our God is saying and then you can tell us whatever he says to you; then we will pay attention and do it.”

eras.label: Era Six · Deuteronomy 6
eras.name: The Shema — Love the LORD With All Your Heart
eras.dates: The single most quoted verse in Judaism opens this chapter — the declaration of God's oneness and the command to love him completely — followed by practical instructions for keeping that love embedded in ordinary daily life.

events.title: "Hear, O Israel" — the Shema
events.detail: Moses delivers the foundational declaration of Israel's faith — the LORD is one, and Israel must love him with everything they have — commanding that these words be taught constantly to children, tied on the hand, and inscribed on doorframes, so obedience becomes woven into daily life rather than a special occasion.

verses.text: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD [Yahweh] is our God [Elohim], the LORD [Yahweh] is one! You must love the LORD [Yahweh] your God [Elohim] with your whole mind, your whole being, and all your strength.”

eras.label: Era Seven · Deuteronomy 7
eras.name: A Holy People, Chosen Not for Merit
eras.dates: God's choice of Israel is explicitly detached from any claim to greatness — they were, if anything, the least numerous of all peoples — and grounded instead purely in God's own love and his ancient promise to their ancestors.

events.title: "Not Because You Were More Numerous"
events.detail: Facing seven nations stronger than themselves, Israel is commanded to show no mercy and make no treaties, but the chapter's real emphasis is theological: Israel's chosen status rests not on size or merit — they were the smallest of all peoples — but purely on God's love and his oath to their ancestors.

verses.text: “It is not because you were more numerous than all the other peoples that the LORD favored and chose you — for in fact you were the least numerous of all peoples. Rather it is because of his love for you.”

eras.label: Era Eight · Deuteronomy 8
eras.name: "Man Does Not Live by Bread Alone"
eras.dates: Moses reframes forty years of wilderness hardship as deliberate discipline rather than punishment — humbling Israel through hunger and manna specifically to teach dependence on God's word, not merely his provision.

events.title: Manna as a Lesson, Not Just a Meal
events.detail: Moses reinterprets the wilderness manna as intentional teaching, not mere survival — God humbled Israel through hunger specifically to prove that people live by every word from God's mouth, not bread alone — then warns that future prosperity carries its own danger: forgetting the source of it entirely.

verses.text: “He humbled you and allowed you to hunger and caused you to eat manna which you had not known… to make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD [Yahweh].”

eras.label: Era Nine · Deuteronomy 9
eras.name: "Not Because of Your Righteousness" — the Golden Calf Recalled
eras.dates: Moses bluntly denies that Israel's coming victory reflects their own goodness — pointing directly to the golden calf disaster as proof of their stubbornness — and recounts the forty days of prostration that alone kept God from destroying the nation.

events.title: "You Are a Stubborn People"
events.detail: Moses insists Israel's coming conquest owes nothing to their own righteousness — the nations' wickedness, not Israel's virtue, is the real cause — and retells the golden calf incident in vivid detail, including his own forty-day prostration pleading for God not to destroy the nation he had just redeemed.

verses.text: “Do not say in your heart… ‘Because of my own righteousness the LORD has brought me here.’ It is because of the wickedness of these nations that the LORD your God is driving them out ahead of you — not because of your righteousness.”

eras.label: Era Ten · Deuteronomy 10
eras.name: New Tablets, and What the LORD Requires
eras.dates: After the broken tablets are replaced, Moses distills the entire law down to a compact, unforgettable summary — a question with a simple answer: what does God actually want from his people?

events.title: "What Does the LORD Your God Require of You?"
events.detail: Moses recounts carving new stone tablets to replace the shattered ones and Levi's appointment to carry the ark, then distills the entire law into one memorable summary question and answer — revere, obey, love, and serve God wholeheartedly — while also commanding love for the foreigner, "because you were foreigners in the land of Egypt."

verses.text: “Now, Israel, what does the LORD [Yahweh] your God [Elohim] require of you except to revere him, to obey all his commandments, to love him, to serve him with all your mind and being, and to keep the LORD's commandments and statutes… for your own good?”

eras.label: Era Eleven · Deuteronomy 11
eras.name: Blessing and Curse Set Before Israel
eras.dates: Moses contrasts Canaan's rain-dependent agriculture with Egypt's irrigated fields, framing the land itself as a place requiring ongoing trust in God — and sets up the entire book's structural climax: a formal choice between blessing and curse to be spoken from two specific mountains.

events.title: A Land That Drinks Rain From Heaven
events.detail: Unlike Egypt's irrigated fields, Canaan depends entirely on seasonal rain — a built-in incentive for ongoing trust in God — and Moses formally sets before Israel "a blessing and a curse," to be pronounced from Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal once they cross the Jordan.

verses.text: “Take note — I am setting before you today a blessing and a curse: the blessing if you take to heart the commandments of the LORD your God that I am giving you today.”

eras.label: Era Twelve · Deuteronomy 12
eras.name: One Place of Worship
eras.dates: Moses commands the complete demolition of Canaanite worship sites and centralizes Israel's own sacrifices at a single location God will choose — ending the free-for-all where "everyone doing what seems best to him" had defined the wilderness years. (Hebrew chapter 12 covers what most English Bibles number as 12:1-31.)

events.title: "Not as We Are Doing Here Today"
events.detail: Every Canaanite worship site must be torn down completely, and Israel's own sacrifices are restricted to one central place God will choose — a deliberate end to the pattern where "everyone doing what seems best to him" defined worship during the wilderness years.

verses.text: “You must not do as we are doing here today, with everyone doing what seems best to him, for you have not yet come to the final stop and inheritance the LORD your God is giving you.”

eras.label: Era Thirteen · Deuteronomy 13
eras.name: False Prophets and Seduction to Idolatry
eras.dates: Even a prophet whose predicted sign comes true must be rejected and executed if he leads Israel toward other gods — a test measuring loyalty rather than raw predictive accuracy, extended even to a beloved family member or an entire seduced city. (Hebrew chapter 13 covers what most English Bibles number as 12:32-13:18.)

events.title: "The LORD Your God Will Be Testing You"
events.detail: Even a prophet whose sign genuinely comes true must be executed if he uses it to lure Israel toward other gods, since such tests exist specifically to reveal whether Israel truly loves God; the same uncompromising standard extends to a seducing family member or an entire city led into apostasy, which must be destroyed completely. (Numbered 12:32-13:18 in most English translations.)

verses.text: “You must not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer, for the LORD your God will be testing you to see if you love him with all your mind and being.”

eras.label: Era Fourteen · Deuteronomy 14
eras.name: Clean and Unclean Food, and Tithes
eras.dates: Dietary law echoing Leviticus reappears alongside a system of tithing designed explicitly to fund both worship and welfare — supporting the landless Levites and, every third year, the poor, the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow directly.

events.title: Clean and Unclean Animals
events.detail: As "a people holy to the LORD," Israel receives dietary restrictions distinguishing clean from unclean animals, birds, and water creatures — largely echoing Leviticus's earlier categories.

events.title: A Tithe That Feeds the Vulnerable
events.detail: Regular tithes support worship at the central sanctuary, but every third year the entire tithe stays local specifically to feed the Levites, resident foreigners, orphans, and widows — welfare built directly into Israel's worship calendar.

eras.label: Era Fifteen · Deuteronomy 15
eras.name: The Sabbatical Year — Debt Release and Freed Servants
eras.dates: Every seventh year cancels debts between fellow Israelites outright, and any Hebrew servant must go free with generous provisions rather than empty-handed — though the option to stay permanently, marked by a pierced ear, remains available to those who choose it.

events.title: "There Should Not Be Any Poor Among You"
events.detail: Every seventh year cancels debts between fellow Israelites entirely, with a stern warning against withholding generosity in anticipation of that cancellation — since refusing a needy neighbor becomes counted as sin.

verses.text: “There will never cease to be some poor people in the land; therefore, I am commanding you to make sure you open your hand to your fellow Israelites who are needy and poor in your land.”

events.title: Freed Servants Sent Away Generously
events.detail: A Hebrew servant's six-year term ends with mandatory freedom and generous provisions from the master's own flock, threshing floor, and winepress — though a servant who genuinely wants to stay permanently may do so, marked by a pierced ear.

eras.label: Era Sixteen · Deuteronomy 16
eras.name: The Three Pilgrim Festivals
eras.dates: Passover, the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Shelters require every Israelite male to appear before God three times a year at the central sanctuary, closing with an instruction to appoint fair judges — and a flat prohibition on sacred poles or pillars near the altar.

events.title: Passover, Weeks, and Shelters
events.detail: Three annual pilgrimage festivals — Passover and Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Shelters — require every Israelite male to appear before God at the central sanctuary, each occasion explicitly including the Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows in the celebration.

events.title: Judges Who Pursue Justice Alone
events.detail: Every town receives appointed judges under strict instructions against bribery or favoritism, closing with a flat ban on sacred poles or stone pillars anywhere near the LORD's altar.

verses.text: “You must pursue justice alone so that you may live and inherit the land the LORD your God is giving you.”

eras.label: Era Seventeen · Deuteronomy 17
eras.name: Judges, Witnesses, and the Law of the King
eras.dates: Two or more witnesses are required for any capital case, and — anticipating a request still generations away — Moses gives detailed restrictions for Israel's future king: no stockpiling horses, wives, or wealth, and a personal copy of the law read daily for life.

events.title: Two or Three Witnesses Required
events.detail: Idolatry within Israel requires careful investigation and multiple witnesses before execution, with the witnesses themselves required to "be first to begin the execution" — a built-in deterrent against false accusation.

events.title: The Law of the Future King
events.detail: Anticipating Israel's eventual request for a king, Moses restricts the office in advance — no accumulating horses, wives, or excessive wealth — and requires the king to personally copy and read the law daily, "so that he will not exalt himself above his fellow citizens."

verses.text: “When he sits on his royal throne he must make a copy of this law on a scroll… It must be with him constantly, and he must read it as long as he lives.”

eras.label: Era Eighteen · Deuteronomy 18
eras.name: Priestly Portions, and "A Prophet Like Me"
eras.dates: Levites receive their livelihood from the people's offerings rather than land, and Moses delivers one of the book's most theologically loaded promises — a future prophet like himself, whom Israel must listen to on pain of direct divine accountability.

events.title: The Levites' Portion, and Forbidden Occult Practices
events.detail: Priests and Levites, owning no land, receive specific portions of every sacrifice as their livelihood; Israel is forbidden from child sacrifice, divination, sorcery, and necromancy — practices explicitly named as reasons God is driving out the nations before them.

events.title: "A Prophet Like Me"
events.detail: Moses promises that God will raise up a future prophet like himself from among Israel's own people, whom the nation must listen to directly — with a built-in test for discerning a genuine prophet from a false one: whether the prediction actually comes true.

verses.text: “I will raise up a prophet like you for them from among their fellow Israelites. I will put my words in his mouth and he will speak to them whatever I command.”

eras.label: Era Nineteen · Deuteronomy 19
eras.name: Cities of Refuge, and the Law of Witnesses
eras.dates: Three — potentially six — cities of refuge protect an accidental killer from vengeance, while a strict two-or-three-witness rule and the principle of "a life for a life" guard against both unpunished murder and unpunished false accusation.

events.title: Refuge for the Accidental, Justice for the Deliberate
events.detail: Cities of refuge protect someone who kills accidentally from a vengeful relative, but offer no protection for premeditated murder; a false witness who tries to frame an innocent person must suffer exactly the penalty he intended for his victim, reinforcing the requirement of two or three witnesses for any conviction.

verses.text: “You must not show pity; the principle will be a life for a life, an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, a hand for a hand, and a foot for a foot.”

eras.label: Era Twenty · Deuteronomy 20
eras.name: Laws of Warfare
eras.dates: Israel's approach to war comes with built-in exemptions for the newly married, the fearful, and those with unfinished homes or vineyards, alongside a surprising environmental protection — even a besieged enemy's fruit trees may not be needlessly destroyed.

events.title: Exemptions From Battle, and Sparing Fruit Trees
events.detail: Before battle, soldiers who have built an undedicated house, planted an unharvested vineyard, become newly engaged, or simply feel afraid may all go home rather than fight; distant cities are offered peace terms first, while Canaan's own cities face total conquest — yet even in siege warfare, fruit trees may not be needlessly destroyed, since "a tree in the field is not human that you should besiege it."

verses.text: “If you besiege a city for a long time while attempting to capture it, you must not chop down its trees, for you may eat fruit from them and should not cut them down. A tree in the field is not human that you should besiege it!”

eras.label: Era Twenty-One · Deuteronomy 21
eras.name: The Unsolved Murder, the Captive Bride, and the Rebellious Son
eras.dates: Three unrelated but morally weighty scenarios — an unsolved killing, a foreign woman taken in war, and a defiantly rebellious son — each receive careful, humanizing procedures rather than simple, brutal defaults.

events.title: Atonement for an Unsolved Murder
events.detail: When a murder victim is found with no known killer, the nearest town's elders perform a ritual breaking a heifer's neck and publicly declaring their innocence — a communal responsibility even for bloodshed no one directly caused.

events.title: A Captive Wife, and a Rebellious Son
events.detail: A foreign woman taken in war receives a full month to mourn before marriage, and cannot afterward be sold or mistreated if rejected; a persistently rebellious son faces the community's most severe penalty, while anyone executed and hung on a tree must still be buried the same day, since "the one who is left exposed on a tree is cursed by God."

verses.text: “His body must not remain all night on the tree; instead you must make certain you bury him that same day, for the one who is left exposed on a tree is cursed by God.”

eras.label: Era Twenty-Two · Deuteronomy 22
eras.name: Neighborly Duties and Sexual Purity Laws
eras.dates: A dense mix of practical neighborliness — returning lost property, helping a fallen animal — sits beside strict sexual purity regulations, evidence for virginity claims, and the tassels commanded back in Numbers. (Hebrew chapter 22 covers what most English Bibles number as 22:1-29.)

events.title: Lost Property, Mixed Kinds, and Sexual Purity
events.detail: Israelites must help recover a neighbor's lost animal or fallen ox, avoid mixing seeds, animals, or fabrics, and wear tassels on their garments; detailed sexual purity laws follow, including required evidence for virginity accusations and severe penalties for adultery and assault, distinguishing cases where a victim could or could not have cried out for help.

eras.label: Era Twenty-Three · Deuteronomy 23
eras.name: Exclusions From the Assembly, and Camp Purity
eras.dates: Certain nations are barred from Israel's worshiping assembly for generations because of how they treated Israel in the wilderness, and camp sanitation rules reflect a startling theological premise — God himself walks through the camp, so nothing indecent can be left in view. (Hebrew chapter 23 covers what most English Bibles number as 23:1-25.)

events.title: "The LORD Your God Walks in the Middle of Your Camp"
events.detail: Opening with a prohibition on marrying a father's former wife, the chapter bars Ammonites and Moabites from Israel's assembly for hiring Balaam to curse them, while even basic camp sanitation — a designated latrine outside camp — is grounded in the striking claim that God himself "walks about in the middle of your camp," so nothing indecent should be visible to him. (Verse 1 numbered 22:30 in most English translations; verses 2-26 numbered 23:1-25.)

verses.text: “The LORD your God walks about in the middle of your camp to deliver you and defeat your enemies for you. Therefore your camp should be holy, so that he does not see anything indecent among you and turn away from you.”

eras.label: Era Twenty-Four · Deuteronomy 24
eras.name: Divorce, and Fair Treatment of the Poor and Vulnerable
eras.dates: A brief regulation permitting divorce documents becomes, centuries later, the very text Jesus's opponents cite against him — while surrounding laws repeatedly protect day laborers, the poor, and the harvest gleanings owed to the vulnerable.

events.title: A Certificate of Divorce, and Protections for the Poor
events.detail: A man who divorces his wife may not remarry her if she has since remarried and been widowed or divorced again — a regulation later central to a New Testament controversy — while surrounding laws repeatedly protect the vulnerable: prompt wages for day laborers, individual accountability instead of generational punishment, and harvest gleanings deliberately left for the foreigner, orphan, and widow.

verses.text: “Whenever you reap your harvest in your field and leave some unraked grain there, you must not return to get it; it should go to the resident foreigner, orphan, and widow.”

eras.label: Era Twenty-Five · Deuteronomy 25
eras.name: Justice, Levirate Marriage, and Remembering Amalek
eras.dates: A capped limit on judicial beatings, the obligation of a brother-in-law to preserve a dead man's family line, and a standing command to blot out Amalek's memory all reflect a society weighing dignity, family continuity, and old grievances at once.

events.title: Capped Punishment, and Honest Weights
events.detail: Judicial beatings are capped at forty blows "so that you might not view your fellow Israelite with contempt," a brother-in-law who refuses to preserve his dead brother's line faces public humiliation, and dishonest weights and measures are declared "abhorrent to the LORD."

events.title: "Blot Out the Memory of Amalek"
events.detail: Moses commands Israel to remember, once settled and secure, how Amalek attacked the weakest stragglers during the exodus — a standing order to eliminate Amalek's memory entirely, later revisited in Saul's reign.

verses.text: “When the LORD your God gives you relief from all the enemies who surround you in the land he is giving you as an inheritance, you must wipe out the memory of the Amalekites from under heaven — do not forget!”

eras.label: Era Twenty-Six · Deuteronomy 26
eras.name: Firstfruits, Tithes, and the Historical Creed
eras.dates: A liturgical formula recited over the first harvest offering compresses Israel's entire national story — a wandering Aramean, slavery in Egypt, and deliverance — into a single memorized confession every worshiper must speak aloud.

events.title: "A Wandering Aramean Was My Ancestor"
events.detail: Presenting the first harvest offering requires reciting a compact historical creed tracing Israel's whole story from Jacob's descent into Egypt through slavery to deliverance, followed by a declaration that Israel and God have mutually bound themselves to one another this very day.

verses.text: “A wandering Aramean was my ancestor, and he went down to Egypt and lived there as a foreigner with a household few in number, but there he became a great, powerful, and numerous people.”

eras.label: Era Twenty-Seven · Deuteronomy 27
eras.name: Stones on Mount Ebal, and the Twelve Curses
eras.dates: Moses instructs a plaster-covered stone monument inscribed with the entire law, then choreographs a dramatic covenant ceremony — six tribes on one mountain, six on another — reciting twelve specific curses that every Israelite must publicly affirm with "Amen."

events.title: Six Tribes, Six Tribes, and Twelve "Amens"
events.detail: Moses commands a plastered stone monument inscribed with the whole law to be erected on Mount Ebal, then divides the twelve tribes between Gerizim for blessing and Ebal for cursing, where the Levites recite twelve specific curses that every Israelite must publicly affirm aloud with "Amen."

eras.label: Era Twenty-Eight · Deuteronomy 28
eras.name: Blessings and Curses in Full
eras.dates: The book's longest chapter lays out covenant consequences at their most extreme — abundant, overflowing blessing for obedience, and a catalog of escalating, horrifying curses for rebellion that reads, by its final verses, like a preview of siege warfare and exile centuries before either happened. (Hebrew chapter 28 covers what most English Bibles number as 28:1-68.)

events.title: Blessings for Obedience
events.detail: Obedience promises blessing in the city and field, in coming and going, over enemies, livestock, and harvest — Israel elevated above every nation on earth, lending to many nations and borrowing from none.

verses.text: “If you indeed obey the LORD [Yahweh] your God [Elohim] and are careful to observe all his commandments I am giving you today, the LORD [Yahweh] your God [Elohim] will elevate you above all the nations of the earth.”

events.title: Curses for Disobedience
events.detail: Disobedience triggers a mirror-image catalog of curses — disease, defeat, drought, madness, and oppression — escalating into horrifying detail, including siege-driven cannibalism, that eerily anticipates the exact fate Jerusalem would suffer centuries later under Babylonian siege.

verses.text: “If you ignore the LORD your God and are not careful to keep all his commandments and statutes I am giving you today, then all these curses will come upon you in full force.”

events.title: Exile, and Slavery Sold Back to Egypt
events.detail: The chapter's darkest closing image reverses the exodus itself — Israel sold back into slavery in Egypt by ship, with no buyer even willing to take them — the ultimate covenant curse for a nation that would not serve God "joyfully and wholeheartedly." (Verse 69 numbered 29:1 in most English translations.)

verses.text: “The LORD will make you return to Egypt by ship, over a route I said to you that you would never see again. There you will sell yourselves to your enemies as male and female slaves, but no one will buy you.”

eras.label: Era Twenty-Nine · Deuteronomy 29
eras.name: The Covenant Renewed in Moab
eras.dates: A second, distinct covenant — beyond the one made at Horeb — binds every Israelite present that day, along with generations not yet born, to the terms Moses has just spelled out in exhaustive detail. (Hebrew chapter 29 covers what most English Bibles number as 29:2-29.)

events.title: A Covenant for Those Not Yet Born
events.detail: Moses formalizes a second covenant in Moab, explicitly binding not just those physically present but future generations as well, warning that any secret idolater who assumes he can escape judgment will instead be singled out for the full weight of every curse written in the scroll. (Numbered 29:2-28 in most English translations.)

events.title: "The Secret Things Belong to the LORD"
events.detail: The chapter closes with a compact statement of epistemic humility — some things remain hidden with God alone, while what has been revealed belongs to Israel to obey. (Numbered 29:29 in most English translations.)

verses.text: “The secret things belong to the LORD [Yahweh] our God [Elohim], but those that are revealed belong to us and our descendants forever, so that we might obey all the words of this law.” (Numbered 29:29 in most English translations.)

eras.label: Era Thirty · Deuteronomy 30
eras.name: "Choose Life" — Return and Restoration
eras.dates: Even after every curse in chapter 28 plays out in full, God promises restoration is still available — genuine return brings gathering from the most distant exile, a circumcised heart, and a final, urgent choice laid before the whole nation.

events.title: "I Have Set Before You Life and Death"
events.detail: Even after exile for covenant-breaking, God promises that genuine repentance will bring restoration "from the most distant land," including a transformed, circumcised heart capable of real love for God — closing with Moses's climactic charge to choose between life and death, blessing and curse.

verses.text: “Today I invoke heaven and earth as witnesses against you that I have set life and death, blessing and curse, before you. Therefore choose life so that you and your descendants may live!”

eras.label: Era Thirty-One · Deuteronomy 31
eras.name: Moses Commissions Joshua, and Writes the Song
eras.dates: At 120 years old and barred from entering Canaan, Moses formally hands leadership to Joshua with a repeated charge to be strong and courageous, then writes a prophetic song specifically because he already knows Israel will eventually break the covenant.

events.title: "Be Strong and Courageous"
events.detail: At 120, Moses publicly commissions Joshua as his successor with a doubled charge to be strong and courageous, and commands the law to be read publicly every seven years so each new generation, including children, learns to fear the LORD.

verses.text: “Be strong and courageous! Do not fear or tremble before them, for the LORD [Yahweh] your God [Elohim] is the one who is going with you. He will not fail you or abandon you!”

events.title: A Song Written as a Future Witness
events.detail: God tells Moses plainly that Israel will eventually abandon the covenant once settled and prosperous, and commands him to compose a song specifically to serve as a witness against the nation when that day comes — a prophecy of failure written down before the failure itself occurs.

verses.text: “Now write down for yourselves the following song and teach it to the Israelites. Put it into their very mouths so that this song may serve as my witness against the Israelites!”

eras.label: Era Thirty-Two · Deuteronomy 32
eras.name: The Song of Moses
eras.dates: Moses's prophetic song recasts Israel's entire future in poetic form — God as a faithful Rock, Israel as an ungrateful, rebellious people who will chase other gods, and a coming judgment that God will nonetheless temper for the sake of his own reputation among the nations.

events.title: "The Rock, His Work Is Perfect"
events.detail: The Song of Moses opens by declaring God's flawless faithfulness as "the Rock" before turning to Israel's ingratitude — a people who grew fat and prosperous, then abandoned the very God who carried them like an eagle bearing its young.

verses.text: “As for the Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are just. He is a reliable God [El] who is never unjust, he is fair and upright.”

events.title: "I Kill and I Give Life"
events.detail: The song closes with God's own declaration of absolute, unrivaled power over life and death, promising eventual vindication for his people even after using foreign nations to discipline them; Moses then climbs Mount Nebo, per God's own instruction, to view the land he will never enter.

verses.text: “See now that I, indeed I, am he, and there is no god with me. I kill and give life, I wound and I heal, and no one can deliver out of my hand.”

eras.label: Era Thirty-Three · Deuteronomy 33
eras.name: Moses Blesses the Twelve Tribes
eras.dates: In his final public act, Moses pronounces individual blessings over each tribe by name — echoing Jacob's own deathbed blessings in Genesis a generation earlier — closing with an exultant declaration of Israel's unique security under God's protection.

events.title: "Who Is Like You, Israel?"
events.detail: Moses blesses each of the twelve tribes individually by name — Reuben, Judah, Levi, Benjamin, Joseph, and the rest — before closing his entire farewell address with an exultant declaration that no other nation enjoys the LORD's kind of unique, victorious protection.

verses.text: “You have joy, Israel! Who is like you? You are a people delivered by the LORD, your protective shield and your exalted sword. May your enemies cringe before you; may you trample on their backs.”

eras.label: Era Thirty-Four · Deuteronomy 34
eras.name: The Death of Moses
eras.dates: From the summit of Mount Nebo, Moses sees the entire promised land laid out before him — and dies there without ever setting foot in it, closing the Torah with the flat statement that no prophet since has known the LORD so directly, face to face.

events.title: "No Prophet Ever Again Arose Like Moses"
events.detail: God shows Moses the whole land from Mount Nebo's summit before Moses dies there at 120, still strong and clear-eyed, buried in an unmarked grave; the Torah closes noting that no prophet since has known the LORD face to face the way Moses did, nor matched his signs, wonders, and "great power and awesome might in view of all Israel."

verses.text: “No prophet ever again arose in Israel like Moses, who knew the LORD [Yahweh] face to face.”
